title: Story or not a story?
instructions: Each line has six words or fewer. Sort them: does it tell a story, or is it just a fact?

items.text: Wrong bus. Right friend. Lucky Tuesday.
Missed the shot. Won anyway. Teamwork.
Dragon egg cracked. Babysitting starts now.

title: Words that carry feeling
instructions: Tap the two words that hint at how the girl feels about moving.
text: Moving day. Empty room. Her drawing stayed.
explanation: "Empty" makes the room feel sad and quiet. "Stayed" suggests she left something important behind, maybe on purpose.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a six-word story?

options.text: Lost dog found. Best day ever.
I went to the park and played on the swings all day.

questions.explanation: It has exactly six words and something happens: a lost dog is found, and there's a feeling too.
questions.hint: Count the words, then ask: does something happen?

questions.prompt: In "Last day of school. Nobody cried.", which word makes you wonder the most?
questions.explanation: Usually someone cries on the last day. "Nobody" surprises us. Was it a bad year? A happy one?

title: Your six-word story
prompt: Write your own six-word story about a surprise, a loss, or a big change. Make every word do a job!
tips: Start in the middle of the action.
Leave the reader with a question.
Try writing three versions, then pick your favorite.

title: Telling or showing?
instructions: Sort each sentence: does it tell the feeling, or show it?

items.text: Ava's eyes kept closing during the movie.
Socks hung from the lamp, and cereal crunched under our feet.
Grandpa held my report card up for the whole street to see.

title: Nervous clues
instructions: Tap the three words that show Priya is nervous.
text: Priya hugged her knees on the bus. Her stomach flipped every time the school came closer.
explanation: Hugging her knees and a flipping stomach are body clues. We feel her nerves without the word "nervous".

questions.prompt: Which sentence SHOWS that Noah is cold?

options.text: Noah's teeth chattered as he pulled his sleeves over his hands.
It was a cold day for Noah.

questions.explanation: Chattering teeth and pulling sleeves over his hands are clues. The other two just say "cold".
questions.hint: Look for actions or body clues, not the word "cold".

questions.prompt: What feeling does this show? "Zoe kept checking the clock and tapping her foot."
questions.explanation: Checking the clock and tapping a foot are things we do while waiting for something to finally happen.

title: Telling → showing
prompt: Turn this telling sentence into showing. Use actions, body language and details so the reader can feel the anger, without naming it.
tips: What does Ava do with her hands? Her face? Her voice?
What does she do to the things around her?
Imagine you're filming it: what would the camera see?

title: Which sense?
instructions: Sort each detail by the sense it uses most.

items.text: a sky the color of orange juice

title: Hear and smell it
instructions: Tap the three words that help you hear or smell this scene.
text: Rain drummed on the tin roof while the sharp smell of wet dirt drifted through the window.
explanation: "Drummed" lets you hear the rain, and the smell of wet dirt puts you right by that window.

questions.prompt: Which sense does this use? "The pavement burned through my thin sneakers."
questions.explanation: You feel the heat through your shoes. That's touch.

questions.prompt: Which sentence describes popcorn without naming it?

options.text: We ate popcorn during the movie.
Buttery puffs crackled in the microwave as a salty smell drifted out.

questions.explanation: It never says "popcorn", but the crackling, the butter and the salty smell tell you exactly what it is.
questions.hint: Which one uses the senses and doesn't say what it is?

title: Mystery description
prompt: Describe a thunderstorm using at least three senses, without naming it. A classmate should be able to guess what you're describing!
tips: What do you hear first? What does the air smell like?
How does the light change? What do you feel on your skin?
Use a comparison: "The sky growled like…"

title: Weak or strong?
instructions: Sort the verbs: weak (tells us little) or strong (paints a picture)?

title: Tired words
instructions: Tap the six weak or tired words a writer could replace.
text: The boy went to the store and got a very good snack. He said it was nice.
explanation: Went, got and said are weak verbs; very, good and nice are vague. Try: "The boy raced to the corner shop and grabbed a cheesy pretzel. 'Best snack ever,' he mumbled."

questions.prompt: Which verb paints the clearest picture? "The puppy ___ under the bed."
questions.explanation: "Scurried" shows quick, tiny steps. You can almost hear the paws.
One strong word (starving) beats "very" + a weak word.
questions.hint: Look for one word that means "very hungry".

title: Power up the paragraph
prompt: Rewrite this flat paragraph with strong verbs and precise words. Add details to make it exciting!
starter: The girl went to the park. It was very nice. She got on the swing and went very high. Then she said it was a good day.
tips: Replace every weak verb (went, got, said) with a strong one.
Swap "very nice" and "good" for precise details.
Give the girl a name and the park a sound or a smell.
